Read measurements and protein estimates

y holds the filtered precursors from 01_Filtering. proteins holds the protein estimates and their standard errors that 02_quantify_run.R saved, because dpcQuant() takes about 100 minutes and this notebook should render in minutes. The checkpoint must come from the current filtered input; nothing in the file ties it to that input, so rerun the script whenever filtering changes.

y <- readRDS(here("01_Preprocess", "01_Filtering", "c_data", "precursors_filtered.rds"))

checkpoints <- here("01_Preprocess", "02_Quantification", "c_data", "quant_runs")
sensitivity_file <- file.path(checkpoints, "proteins_slope_fitted.rds")
proteins <- readRDS(file.path(checkpoints, "proteins_slope_0.7.rds"))

Missingness

In DIA data, low-intensity precursors go missing more often. The plot takes the precursor matrix and shows the proportion of missing values against mean observed intensity; a downward trend is that association. It does not show why a given value is missing.

plotAveVsMis(y)

Fit the detection curve

The detection probability curve (DPC) gives the probability that a precursor is observed as a function of its true intensity, through an intercept and a slope. dpc() takes the log2 matrix and returns the fitted pair. Its default, model = "cn", is dpcCN(), the complete-normal estimator the limpa FAQ recommends for noisy data, fitted on a stratified subset of 2,000 precursors.

dpcest <- dpc(y$E)
plotDPC(dpcest)
dpc_parameters <- tibble(intercept = dpcest$dpc[1], slope = dpcest$dpc[2])
round(dpc_parameters, 3)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  intercept slope
      <dbl> <dbl>
1     -8.96 0.488

The fitted slope, 0.488, sits below the 0.7 to 0.9 band the limpa FAQ calls typical for DIA-NN with match-between-runs. The FAQ’s advice for that case is the project’s choice for the primary run: “If dpcCN() doesn’t give a value in that range, it would be reasonable to run dpcQuant() with a preset value dpc.slope=0.7.” Standard errors or hit counts alone do not show which slope is right, so the fitted slope is kept as a sensitivity run (below and in 02_Differential).

Roll-up

02_quantify_run.R combines precursors into proteins with dpcQuant(), grouping by Protein.Group. It returns a complete matrix, an abundance for every protein in every sample, plus a standard error per value that dpcDE() later uses as a precision weight. The loaded checkpoint holds 3,451 protein groups from 47,133 precursors.

Detection filter

filterByDetection() takes the protein object and a minimum number of samples, and returns one TRUE or FALSE per protein. For a small experiment its help page sets n.samples to the smallest group size. The count runs across all samples, so it does not guarantee detection within any one group.

group_sizes <- table(proteins$targets$group)
detected <- filterByDetection(proteins, n.samples = min(group_sizes))
proteins <- proteins[detected, ]

group_sizes

 BFR_T1  BFR_T2 HLRT_T1 HLRT_T2 
     33      32      33      33 
c(before = length(detected), kept = sum(detected), dropped = sum(!detected))

   3451    3042     409

Normalisation

Cyclic loess (normalizeBetweenArrays(method = "cyclicloess")) removes abundance-dependent differences between samples. DIA-NN normalised the precursors already; this second pass works on the protein estimates. Smyth recommends quantile or cyclic loess normalisation of limpa protein quantifications when sample differences are technical (Bioconductor support).

Two helpers describe the effect. An MA curve plots a sample’s difference from the across-sample mean against average abundance. ma_width() takes a log2 matrix and returns, per sample, the range of its fitted MA curve; a large range means the difference changes with abundance. spread() returns the range of sample medians. Both describe; neither decides whether normalisation is right.

ma_width <- function(m) {
  a <- rowMeans(m)
  apply(m, 2, function(x) diff(range(lowess(a, x - a, f = 0.5)$y)))
}
spread <- function(m) diff(range(apply(m, 2, median)))

unnormalised <- proteins$E
widths <- ma_width(unnormalised)
before <- c(ma_width = median(widths), median_spread = spread(unnormalised))
proteins$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(proteins$E, method = "cyclicloess")
after <- c(ma_width = median(ma_width(proteins$E)), median_spread = spread(proteins$E))

round(rbind(before, after), 3)
       ma_width median_spread
before    0.448         1.175
after     0.161         0.430

Intensity distributions before and after, then the sample with the widest MA curve before and after.

worst <- which.max(widths)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plotDensities(unnormalised, legend = FALSE, main = "Before cyclic loess")
plotDensities(proteins$E, legend = FALSE, main = "After cyclic loess")
plotMD(unnormalised, column = worst, main = paste(colnames(unnormalised)[worst], "before"))
plotMD(proteins$E, column = worst, main = paste(colnames(proteins$E)[worst], "after"))

Only proteins$E changes. The standard errors stay on the unnormalised scale, and dpcDE() reads them as if they matched; the mapping is close to linear, but this approximation carries into every later stage.

Check protein estimates

Per protein: precursor count (NPrec, which dpcQuant() writes although its help page says NPeptides), proportion observed, mean log2 abundance and mean standard error.

protein_quality <- tibble(
  protein = rownames(proteins),
  gene = proteins$genes$Genes,
  n_precursors = proteins$genes$NPrec,
  prop_observed = proteins$genes$PropObs,
  mean_log2 = rowMeans(proteins$E),
  mean_standard_error = rowMeans(proteins$other$standard.error),
  mean_n_observations = rowMeans(proteins$other$n.observations)
)
summary(protein_quality[c("mean_log2", "mean_standard_error", "prop_observed")])
   mean_log2     mean_standard_error prop_observed    
 Min.   :12.98   Min.   :0.03107     Min.   :0.03716  
 1st Qu.:16.07   1st Qu.:0.38500     1st Qu.:0.30245  
 Median :17.10   Median :0.58428     Median :0.42324  
 Mean   :17.53   Mean   :0.65862     Mean   :0.43278  
 3rd Qu.:18.63   3rd Qu.:0.91420     3rd Qu.:0.54962  
 Max.   :26.79   Max.   :1.50131     Max.   :0.97710

plotMDSUsingSEs() places samples by their protein profiles, weighting by the standard errors; colour is participant. A sample far from its own participant’s other samples is worth a look. r2() takes a factor and returns the share of the first coordinate it explains, for participant and group separately.

mds <- plotMDSUsingSEs(proteins, pch = 16, col = as.integer(factor(proteins$targets$participant)))
r2 <- function(f) summary(lm(mds$x ~ factor(f)))$r.squared
round(map_dbl(proteins$targets[c("participant", "group")], r2), 3)
participant       group 
      0.515       0.027

Slope sensitivity

The sensitivity run quantifies against the whole fitted curve, where the primary run passes dpc.slope = 0.7 and lets limpa fit the intercept. Both get the same detection filter and normalisation. The table compares protein counts and mean standard errors on shared proteins; the median absolute abundance difference follows. It measures how far values move, not whether the contrasts change; 02_Differential compares those.

sensitivity <- readRDS(sensitivity_file)
sensitivity <- sensitivity[filterByDetection(sensitivity, n.samples = min(group_sizes)), ]
sensitivity$E <- normalizeBetweenArrays(sensitivity$E, method = "cyclicloess")

shared <- intersect(rownames(proteins), rownames(sensitivity))
tibble(
  slope = c(0.7, round(dpcest$dpc[2], 3)),
  role = c("primary", "sensitivity"),
  n_proteins = c(nrow(proteins), nrow(sensitivity)),
  n_shared = length(shared),
  mean_standard_error = round(c(
    mean(proteins$other$standard.error[shared, ]),
    mean(sensitivity$other$standard.error[shared, ])
  ), 3)
)
# A tibble: 2 × 5
  slope role        n_proteins n_shared mean_standard_error
  <dbl> <chr>            <int>    <int>               <dbl>
1 0.7   primary           3042     3042               0.659
2 0.488 sensitivity       3042     3042               0.532
round(median(abs(proteins$E[shared, ] - sensitivity$E[shared, ])), 4)
[1] 0.2373

The section runs only when c_data/quant_runs/proteins_slope_fitted.rds exists. It takes a separate quantification run:

Rscript 01_Preprocess/02_Quantification/a_script/02_quantify_run.R --sensitivity

Save results

proteins.rds keeps abundance, standard errors, annotations and sample metadata together for every later stage. 02_quantify.xlsx holds the samples, the fitted curve, detection counts, the normalisation summary and per-protein quality.

sheets <- list(
  samples = as.data.frame(proteins$targets),
  dpc_parameters = dpc_parameters,
  detection_summary = data.frame(
    before = length(detected), kept = sum(detected), dropped = sum(!detected),
    minimum_samples = min(group_sizes)
  ),
  normalisation_summary = data.frame(
    stage = c("before", "after"), rbind(before, after), row.names = NULL
  ),
  protein_quality = protein_quality
)
overview <- data.frame(
  sheet = names(sheets), rows = map_int(sheets, nrow), columns = map_int(sheets, ncol),
  description = c(
    "Sample identifiers and study metadata",
    "Fitted diagnostic DPC; primary quantification uses preset slope 0.7",
    "Protein counts and minimum sample threshold for detection filtering",
    "Median MA-curve range and sample-median spread before and after normalisation",
    "Per-protein coverage, abundance and standard error"
  )
)

out <- here("01_Preprocess", "02_Quantification", "c_data")
saveRDS(proteins, file.path(out, "proteins.rds"))
write_xlsx(c(list(overview = overview), sheets), file.path(out, "02_quantify.xlsx"))
